Why does an MLP with no activation functions collapse to a linear model?
column2: A composition of affine maps is affine: \(W_2(W_1x + b_1) + b_2 = (W_2W_1)x + (W_2b_1+b_2)\). The demo checks this numerically.

column1:
DL-01 · self-check
Walk through the backward pass for L = (w·x + b − y)², one node at a time.
column2: Forward: \(u = w^\top x\), \(v = u + b\), \(e = v - y\), \(L = e^2\). Backward: \(\partial L/\partial e = 2e\); \(\partial L/\partial v = 2e\); \(\partial L/\partial b = 2e\); \(\partial L/\partial u = 2e\); \(\partial L/\partial w = 2e\,x\). This is the CORE-02 gradient for a single example.

column1:
DL-01 · self-check
Why do we accumulate (+=) gradients in micrograd instead of assigning them?
column2: A value used in several places receives gradient from each path, and the multivariate chain rule sums them. Assigning would keep only the last path. Example: \(x\cdot x\) needs \(2x\), and assignment would give \(x\).

column1:
DL-01 · self-check
Show that minimizing cross-entropy is the same as maximizing likelihood under a categorical model.
column2: The likelihood of the labels is \(\prod_i p_{y_i}(x_i)\), so the NLL is \(-\sum_i\log p_{y_i}(x_i)\), which is exactly the sum of cross-entropies between the one-hot labels and the predicted distributions. Same objective, same minimizer.

column1:
DL-01 · self-check
What's the computational cost of backprop compared with a forward pass, and why is it so cheap?
column2: About 2× the forward pass (two matmuls per layer: one for the weight gradient, one to propagate the error), so about 3× in total, independent of the number of parameters. It's cheap because reverse mode reuses the stored intermediate values and computes all the parameter gradients in one sweep. The cost is memory for the activations.

column2: Gradient-check layer by layer, in float64, on a tiny input, with randomness off. Look for transposes, a missing \(1/B\), = vs += for reused values, an activation derivative computed on the wrong tensor, or a check that sits exactly on the ReLU kink (§5).

DL-02 · self-check
What's the difference between tensor.view and tensor.reshape? When does view fail?
column2: view reinterprets the existing memory without copying, so it needs a stride-compatible layout. It fails on non-contiguous tensors (after transpose/permute, for example). reshape falls back to a copy when needed.

column1:
DL-02 · self-check
Why do you need optimizer.zero_grad() every step?
column2: backward() adds into .grad, so without zeroing, each step uses the sum of the current and all previous gradients. It's only correct to skip it deliberately, for gradient accumulation.

column1:
DL-02 · self-check
What do model.eval() and torch.no_grad() each do? Why do you usually want both at inference?
column2: eval() changes layer behaviour (dropout off, BatchNorm uses running statistics). no_grad() stops autograd recording (it saves memory and time). They're independent, and inference wants both.

column1:
DL-02 · self-check
What happens if your model is on GPU and your batch is on CPU?
column2: A RuntimeError about tensors being on different devices. Move each batch with .to(device), and remember that .to returns a new tensor.

DL-02 · self-check
(debug) Training loss drops but validation accuracy stays at chance level. Name three PyTorch-specific bugs that cause this.
column2: (1) Labels misaligned with inputs (separate shuffling, or a wrong index in __getitem__). (2) Validation preprocessing differs from training (different normalization, missing transform), or validation runs in train mode with BatchNorm and tiny batches. (3) Evaluating the wrong thing: argmax over the wrong dimension, comparing against the wrong label tensor, or a stale or uninitialized model. Also check for the (N,1) vs (N,) broadcasting bug in a custom loss or metric.

DL-03 · self-check
Why does He initialization scale by sqrt(2/fan_in) for ReLU networks?
column2: \(\operatorname{Var}(a) = n_\text{in}\operatorname{Var}(w)\mathbb{E}[x^2]\), and ReLU makes \(\mathbb{E}[x^2] = \tfrac12\operatorname{Var}(a_\text{prev})\). Preserving the variance layer to layer needs \(\operatorname{Var}(w) = 2/n_\text{in}\) (§1.1). The demo shows a stable std after 50 layers.

column1:
DL-03 · self-check
What problem does BatchNorm solve, and why does it behave differently in train and eval mode?
column2: It stabilizes each layer's input statistics and smooths the landscape, allowing higher learning rates and faster training. In training it uses the batch's statistics. At eval it uses running averages, so outputs are deterministic and don't depend on the other examples in the batch.

column1:
DL-03 · self-check
AdamW vs Adam + L2: what's the difference, and why does it matter?
column2: L2 adds \(\lambda\theta\) to the gradient, which Adam then divides by \(\sqrt{\hat v}\), so parameters with large gradients decay less. AdamW decays the weights directly, uniformly, outside the adaptive scaling. That's better regularization and generalization (see the demo).

column1:
DL-03 · self-check
Why use learning-rate warmup with Adam and large batches?
column2: Early second-moment estimates are based on few samples and are unreliable, and the initial landscape is chaotic. Large learning rates (typical with large batches) can then take destructive steps. Warmup ramps the learning rate up while the statistics and the network settle.

column1:
DL-03 · self-check
What should the loss be at initialization for a 10-class softmax classifier, and why check it?
column2: About \(\ln 10 \approx 2.30\), for near-uniform predictions. Check it to catch overconfident initial logits (fix by scaling down the last layer) and wrong losses or labels.

column1:
DL-03 · self-check
(debug) You can't overfit a single batch of 32 examples. What does that tell you, and what do you check first?
column2: There's a bug in the model or pipeline, not a generalization problem. Check: the labels align with the inputs, the loss gets logits, zero_grad/backward/step are all called, the parameters are actually in the optimizer, nothing is unintentionally frozen, and the learning rate is reasonable.

DL-04 · self-check
A 3×3 conv with 64 input and 128 output channels: how many parameters does it have? How many would a dense layer on a 32×32×64 input need?
column2: \(9\cdot64\cdot128 + 128 = 73{,}856\). A dense layer from 32×32×64 to an output of the same size has about \(8.6\times10^9\) weights. Weight sharing and locality make the difference.

column1:
DL-04 · self-check
Why do stacked 3×3 convs beat one 7×7 conv?
column2: The same 7×7 receptive field with \(27C^2\) instead of \(49C^2\) parameters, plus three non-linearities instead of one, so it's more expressive and cheaper.

column1:
DL-04 · self-check
What problem do residual connections solve, and why do they make very deep networks trainable?
column2: Vanishing gradients and degradation in very deep networks. The identity path makes the block Jacobian \(I + \partial F/\partial x\), so gradients flow back undiminished, and unneeded blocks can learn to be the identity (DL-03 §1.2).

column1:
DL-04 · self-check
When fine-tuning, why freeze early layers first, and why use a smaller learning rate for pretrained weights?
column2: The random new head would send large, noisy gradients into good pretrained features. Freezing protects them while the head learns. Later, small learning rates adapt the features gently without catastrophic forgetting. Early layers are generic, so they need the least change.

column1:
DL-04 · self-check
(debug) Your fine-tuned model scores 98% on validation but fails on photos from users' phones. What's likely going on, and how do you test your guess?
column2: Domain shift: validation came from the training distribution, and phone photos differ (lighting, blur, angle, compression). Test it by labeling a small set of real phone photos and evaluating on them. Fix it by adding such data, using matching augmentation, and monitoring the inputs.

DL-05 · self-check
Why does king − man + woman ≈ queen work, and why shouldn't you over-read it?
column2: Consistent relations are encoded as roughly constant offset directions, because the words' contexts differ in consistent ways. But the inputs are excluded from the search, many analogies fail, the results are cherry-picked, and biases are encoded too.

column1:
DL-05 · self-check
What is perplexity, intuitively, and how does it relate to cross-entropy loss?
column2: \(\text{PPL} = e^{\text{cross-entropy}}\): the effective number of equally likely choices per token. Lower is better. Uniform over \(V\) gives \(V\). It's only comparable for the same tokenizer.

column1:
DL-05 · self-check
In makemore's MLP, what does the embedding table C learn? Why does sharing it across positions matter?
column2: A vector per character, placed so that characters which behave similarly as context are close together. Sharing it across positions means every occurrence trains the same vector, and knowledge transfers between positions and to unseen contexts.

column1:
DL-05 · self-check
Why do vanilla RNNs have trouble learning dependencies 100 steps back?
column2: The gradient passes through a product of 100 Jacobians \(\operatorname{diag}(\tanh')W_h\). With a spectral radius below 1 it shrinks exponentially, so the long-range signal vanishes (the demo shows a norm of about \(10^{-18}\) after 60 steps at \(\rho = 0.5\)).

column1:
DL-05 · self-check
In a seq2seq model, what information is lost by compressing the whole input into one vector?
column2: Everything that doesn't fit in one fixed-size vector: fine details, especially from early or long inputs, get overwritten. Attention removes the bottleneck by letting each decoder step read all the encoder states.

column1:
DL-05 · self-check
(debug) Your character-level LM generates the same letter over and over. What sampling or training issues might cause this?
column2: Greedy or very low-temperature decoding, an undertrained model collapsing onto frequent characters, a bug in feeding the sampled token back in, or a context-length mismatch between training and sampling (§2.4).

column1:
DL-06 · self-check
Why divide by sqrt(d_k) in scaled dot-product attention?
column2: Dot products of \(d_k\)-dimensional vectors with unit-variance entries have variance \(d_k\). Unscaled, the softmax saturates (nearly one-hot) and its gradients vanish. Scaling restores unit variance (§1.1). The demo shows the max-softmax near 1 for raw scores at large \(d_k\).

column1:
DL-06 · self-check
What does the causal mask do, and why is it needed for training a decoder in parallel?
column2: It sets the weights to future positions to 0, so each position conditions only on its prefix. Then one forward pass yields correct next-token predictions for all \(T\) positions at once (teacher forcing in parallel), instead of \(T\) sequential steps.

column1:
DL-06 · self-check
Self-attention is permutation-equivariant. Why does that force us to add positional information?
column2: Attention treats its input as a set: permuting the tokens just permutes the outputs, so word order is invisible. Positions (learned, sinusoidal, RoPE) are needed to tell "dog bites man" from "man bites dog".

column1:
DL-06 · self-check
What's the time and memory cost of attention with respect to sequence length? Why does that matter for long contexts?
column2: \(O(T^2 d)\) time and \(O(T^2)\) memory per head for the score matrix. Long contexts become expensive quadratically, which motivates FlashAttention, sparse or sliding windows, linear attention, and SSMs, and makes the KV cache the inference bottleneck.

column1:
DL-06 · self-check
What role does the residual stream play? What would break without residual connections?
column2: It's a shared channel that every sub-layer reads from and adds to, giving an identity path for gradients and letting layers make incremental edits. Without it, deep transformers suffer vanishing gradients and every layer must re-encode everything.

column1:
DL-06 · self-check
(debug) Your mini-GPT's training loss drops fast but the samples are gibberish, and validation loss is rising. What's happening?
column2: Overfitting: memorizing a small corpus. Use early stopping on validation loss, dropout, weight decay, a smaller model or more data, and check the train/validation split for leakage.

column1:
DL-07 · self-check
What is arithmetic intensity, and why is a big matmul compute-bound while an elementwise op is memory-bound?
column2: AI = FLOPs per byte moved. A matmul does \(O(n^3)\) work on \(O(n^2)\) data, so its AI grows with \(n\) (about \(n/3\) in BF16), above the GPU's ridge point. An elementwise op does about 1 FLOP per 8 bytes, far below the ridge, so it waits on memory.

column1:
DL-07 · self-check
Why does fusing x.cos().cos() into one kernel help, even though the FLOP count is identical?
column2: Unfused, it moves data 4 times (read, write the temporary, read the temporary, write). Fused, it moves data twice. Memory-bound ops take time proportional to the bytes moved, so fusion is about 2× faster for the same arithmetic.

column1:
DL-07 · self-check
BF16 vs FP16: why does BF16 usually not need loss scaling?
column2: It has FP32's 8-bit exponent, so it has the same dynamic range, and small gradients don't underflow. FP16's 5-bit exponent can't represent values below about \(6\times10^{-5}\) as normal numbers, hence loss scaling.

column1:
DL-07 · self-check
Estimate the training memory for a 1B-parameter model with AdamW in mixed precision (parameters + gradients + optimizer state).
column2: About 16 bytes/param: 2 (BF16 weights) + 2 (BF16 gradients) + 4 (FP32 master) + 4 + 4 (Adam m, v). That's about 16 GB, plus activations, which depend on batch size, sequence length, and checkpointing.

column1:
DL-07 · self-check
What does gradient checkpointing trade off?
column2: Extra compute (recomputing the forward pass of the checkpointed segments during backward, roughly +30%) for a large reduction in stored activation memory.

(debug) GPU utilization sits at 35% during training. What are the three most likely culprits, and how do you tell them apart?
column2: (1) The data loader: time it alone, and look for GPU idle gaps while the CPU workers are busy. (2) Sync and Python overhead: .item()/print calls and many tiny kernels, which show as gaps and sync calls in the profiler. (3) Inefficient kernels: the profiler's top ops are unfused or FP32. Fixes are in §4.

DL-08 · self-check
Why does RoPE encode relative position even though it's applied to each token independently?
column2: Rotating \(q\) by \(m\theta\) and \(k\) by \(n\theta\) makes their dot product \(q^\top R_{(n-m)\theta}k\), because rotations compose and transpose to their inverses. The absolute angles cancel, leaving the offset. The demo shows equal scores at equal offsets.

column1:
DL-08 · self-check
How much does GQA with 8 KV heads (out of 32 query heads) shrink the KV cache?
column2: 4×: the cache scales with the number of KV heads (32 → 8). In the example, 2.1 GB becomes 0.54 GB per 4k-token sequence.

column1:
DL-08 · self-check
An MoE model has 47B total and 13B active parameters. What does each number determine: memory, compute, or quality?
column2: Total sets the memory (all the experts must be resident). Active sets the FLOPs per token, and so the compute cost and latency. Quality usually lands between the dense models of each size.

column1:
DL-08 · self-check
Why do MoE models need a load-balancing loss? What happens without it?
column2: Routing is self-reinforcing: experts that get more tokens improve and attract more. Without balancing, the router collapses onto a few experts, the rest are wasted, and tokens are dropped at capacity limits. The auxiliary loss \(E\sum f_iP_i\) pushes toward uniform use (the demo compares token fractions with and without it).

column1:
DL-08 · self-check
What makes Mamba's "selective" SSM different from S4, and why does that matter for language?
column2: S4's parameters are fixed (time-invariant), so it's a convolution, but it can't adapt to content. Mamba makes \(\bar B\), \(C\) and \(\Delta\) depend on the input, so it can choose to store or ignore tokens: content-based selection, needed for language. It's computed with a parallel scan instead of a convolution.

column1:

column2: Check that the auxiliary balance loss is applied with a sensible coefficient, log the per-expert utilization, add the router z-loss and keep the router in FP32, review the capacity factor and dropped tokens, and lower the learning rate or add warmup.

column1:
DL-09 · self-check
What does one message-passing layer compute for a node? What do K layers give it access to?
column2: Each node aggregates (permutation-invariantly) messages from its neighbours and combines them with its own state through shared weights. \(K\) layers give each node information from its \(K\)-hop neighbourhood.

column1:
DL-09 · self-check
How do GCN, GraphSAGE, and GAT differ in how they aggregate neighbours?
column2: GCN: a fixed, symmetric degree-normalized average including self-loops. GraphSAGE: concatenates self with a (sampled) neighbour mean, max, or LSTM aggregate, and is inductive. GAT: learned, input-dependent attention weights over neighbours.

column1:
DL-09 · self-check
What is over-smoothing, and why does it limit GNN depth?
column2: Repeated normalized averaging drives node representations toward the same vector (the top eigenvector of \(\hat A\)), so they lose discriminative information as layers are added. The demo shows the cosine distance collapsing and accuracy falling with depth.

column1:
DL-09 · self-check
Why can't a standard message-passing GNN distinguish some non-isomorphic graphs? What's the connection to the WL test?
column2: An MPNN's update is a (soft) version of 1-WL colour refinement, so it can't separate graphs that 1-WL can't. Example: two triangles vs a 6-cycle (all nodes look identical locally). Mean and max aggregators are even weaker than sum.

column1:
DL-09 · self-check
How is a transformer a GNN on a complete graph? What replaces the adjacency matrix?
column2: Every token aggregates from every other token, with learned attention weights \(\operatorname{softmax}(q^\top k)\) replacing the fixed adjacency. Masks define the graph (a causal mask is a DAG), and positional encodings supply the structure.

column1:
DL-09 · self-check
(debug) Your GCN's validation accuracy peaks at 2 layers and collapses at 8. What's happening, and what can you try?
column2: Over-smoothing (and harder optimization). Use 2–3 layers with residual or jumping-knowledge connections, PairNorm, or DropEdge. For long-range needs, add virtual nodes or use a graph transformer instead of stacking more layers.
